The best prompt I ever wrote was a complete mess.

No framework. No role assignment. No carefully structured context.
Just everything in my head, dumped into the chat without editing.

Here's what I've figured out:

When you try to "craft" the perfect prompt, you edit out the context that matters.
You trim the parts that feel obvious.
You tighten it up so much that you remove the thing Claude actually needed to help you.

A brain dump doesn't do that.
The confusion is in there. The backstory is in there. The real stakes are in there.
And that's exactly what a good AI response needs.

Claude doesn't need your polish. It needs your honesty.

DO THIS:
Next time you're stuck on something, don't write a prompt.
Open Claude and just start talking — like you're explaining the situation to someone who actually has time to hear all of it.
Dump everything. The context, the frustration, what you've already tried, what you're actually trying to accomplish.

Get this:
An output that's actually useful, because it's responding to your real problem — not the cleaned-up version you thought you were supposed to present.
Messy in. Useful out. Every time.

items.content:
AI replacing your sales team is the wrong goal. Here's what the right goal looks like.

My client, a service based business on the east coast, recently laid out his dream of AI handling every sales call, closing every deal — not to cut staff, but to multiply force. Well-intentioned. Well crafted strategy - except for one glaring weakness...

Service businesses are human-delivered. AI is smart, consistent and increasingly persuasive but it's not alive and it's not perfect. The risk here is the AI promising or insinuating a deliverable that is out of scope or flat out wrong.

The smarter play keeps humans at two critical points:

1. A team member quality-checks AI outputs daily — as a routine part of their day, not a bottleneck before every message.

2. A human closer verifies every promise pre-payment, pre-fulfillment — making sure what's being pitched aligns with what you can actually deliver. That's what keeps your brand and your future customer on the same page.

Full automation of sales when humans deliver the service is a fast track to an inevitable credibility risk. My client just avoided it. Yours can too.

items.content:
This week I’m in NYC at HFS Research’s “How to AI” Summit.

HFS founder Phil Fersht kicked things off with a keynote that weaved together their research data and their real world experience helping companies in their AI transformation journeys.

Some data points from Phil’s keynote that stood out:

Only 13% of Global 2000 companies have reached real AI maturity across any of their implementations. 87% are still experimenting.

The companies with lower AI maturity are planning 28% workforce cuts.

The companies with higher AI maturity are planning only 2% cuts, and 37% of them actually expect workforce growth.

Less mature organizations seem to be approaching AI primarily as a cost efficiency lever: reduce labor, lower spend, automate tasks.

More mature organizations appear to be using AI as a value creation lever: increase capacity, redesign work, improve decisions, and create growth.

For procurement, this should shape how we think about:

- business cases for AI
- services and outsourcing strategy
- whether AI is just a cost takeout tool or a driver of enterprise value
- how we evaluate supplier innovation
- what outcomes we should actually be buying

Another stat that stood out: 75% of enterprises are looking to replace services with AI solutions in the next 2–3 years, while three-quarters of BPO and IT services contracts are already being renegotiated because of AI.

Procurement has a front row seat to this transformation, and as such we have influence is helping shape enterprise AI strategy. 

For us, the goal should be to help shift the conversation from “Where can AI help us do the same work cheaper?” To “How can AI help us create more value?”

I’m looking forward to hearing more from practitioners over the next couple of days!

What I took away from this conversation is that procurement has yet another important opportunity to redefine our role in the business, but doing so will require a whole lot more than digital transformation or new tech adoption.

And of course, we wouldn't be able to host an event like this without our partners.  At Catalyst, our partners are experts too.  We break down the buyer/seller silos to create an environment where we can all learn from each other.

Thanks to the leadership of Jim Cahalan and the entire AOP team, I got to show up and participate rather than feel the minute-by-minute stress of all the operational micro-decisions that have to be made on the day to make an event like this a success. 

And finally, to those who invested a day of their precious time AND joined us ready to be open, vulnerable, and learn... Catalyst couldn't be Catalyst without it!

So, thank you San Francisco... we'll be back next year. 

And next up -> Detroit and New York City!

items.content:
Spend analytics has come a long way from spreadsheets, but many organizations still struggle to describe what “good” actually looks like. 
🎧 https://lnkd.in/eXPrP6sh

Without a clear benchmark, it is easy to assume performance is strong when there are still meaningful opportunities left untapped.

In this week’s podcast episode, Kelly Barner and I talk with Sammeli Sammalkorpi, Co-Founder and CEO of Sievo, to explore insights drawn from $1.4 trillion in procurement spend, as outlined in their annual State of Spend report. 

Our conversation challenges some long-held assumptions, particularly around control. We discussed whether policies like ‘no PO, no pay’ always serve the intended purpose, and how procurement leaders can take a more nuanced approach depending on the category and business context. 

Procurement’s ability to create impact is closely tied to how well they understand their own performance in context. When that context is grounded in data, it becomes much easier to move from assumption to action.
